title: SAME-R: smoke particle size, aging and detector response in microgravity
summary: 47 smoke tests from the 2010 ISS reflight of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment were organised. Smoke from overheated spacecraft materials was aged and sent past particle instruments and real ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors. The analysis reproduces NASA's particle sizes, quantifies Brownian coagulation and shows that light-scattering and ionization detectors fail in opposite conditions. An AutoResearch-selected model predicts particle size and detector response from the test conditions.

scope.setting: Microgravity Science Glovebox on the International Space Station, July–September 2010.
scope.note: All tests come from one flight and one hardware set; they are not independent flights.

measurements.label: Particle number concentration (M0)
measurements.result: 0.56–5.0 million particles per cm³ with flow; 0.15–0.50 million without flow.
measurements.why_it_matters: Zeroth moment; with M1 and M3 it gives the mean sizes.

measurements.label: Diameter concentration (M1)
measurements.result: Count mean diameter AMD = M1/M0 of 0.05–0.45 µm.
measurements.why_it_matters: Proportional to the signal of an ionization smoke detector.

measurements.label: Mass concentration (M3)
measurements.result: Diameter of average mass Dm = (M3/M0)^1/3 of 0.09–0.93 µm.
measurements.why_it_matters: Related to what light-scattering detectors see.

measurements.label: Aging time
measurements.result: Unaged pushes 36–40 s after the fill; aged pushes 211–1913 s.
measurements.why_it_matters: Stands in for smoke transport time from source to detector.

measurements.label: ISS smoke detector (photoelectric)
measurements.result: Responded to 71% of pushes with flow and 90% without.
measurements.why_it_matters: The detector type flying on the ISS.

measurements.label: Ionization chamber
measurements.result: Responded to 93% of pushes with flow and 10% without.
measurements.why_it_matters: Same principle as the Space Shuttle detector.

moment_method.rule: Three instruments measure three moments of the size distribution: M0 (count), M1 (count × diameter) and M3 (count × diameter³). AMD = M1/M0 and Dm = (M3/M0)^1/3 need no assumption; assuming a log-normal shape, σg = exp(√ln(Dm/AMD)) and Dg = AMD / exp(½ ln²σg).

real_example.plain_explanation: 3.9 million particles per cm³ averaging 0.21 µm across; the mass-weighted size is 0.39 µm, so the spread is wide (σg 2.2) and the typical (median) particle is 0.15 µm.

moment_method.interpretation_limit: Moments are NASA/NIST-calibrated values; raw instrument voltages are not re-calibrated here.

detector_comparison.meaning: Light scattering misses small (≈0.1 µm) Kapton/Teflon smoke in ventilated air; ionization misses dilute coarse smoke made in still air.

coagulation.meaning: Particles collide and merge; after ~10 minutes about 60% of them are gone and the rest are larger.

insights.title: Published SAME-2 particle sizes reproduced
insights.evidence: The moment-method statistics re-derived here match the published SAME-2 Table 1: the diameter of average mass agrees within 11% for all 10 material × aging cases.
insights.meaning: The extraction and moment calculations are consistent with NASA's analysis.
insights.why_it_matters: Builds trust in every derived number shown on the dashboard.

insights.title: Wire insulation makes the smallest smoke
insights.evidence: Kapton and Teflon (wire-insulation polymers) produce the smallest smoke: Dm 0.10–0.23 µm, versus 0.29–0.56 µm for lampwick (cellulose), Pyrell foam and silicone rubber at 8 cm/s flow.
insights.meaning: Kapton and Teflon smoke is mostly below 0.2 µm.
insights.why_it_matters: Electrical overheating of wiring is a leading spacecraft fire precursor.

insights.title: Smoke grows while it travels
insights.evidence: With flow, 527–793 s of extra aging cut the particle count to 27%–50% of its initial value and grew Dm by ×1.25–1.56. The growth equals the mass-conserving coagulation prediction (N0/N)^1/3, giving a coagulation coefficient of 9.0e-10 cm³/s, consistent with NASA's note (1.2e-09–1.7e-09) and Brownian theory.
insights.meaning: Brownian coagulation removes small particles and enlarges the rest.
insights.why_it_matters: The size a detector sees depends on how long the smoke took to reach it.

insights.title: Aging narrows the distribution
insights.evidence: Aging narrowed the size distribution (σg fell) in 11 of 12 flow runs, the trend expected as coagulating smoke approaches a self-preserving distribution.
insights.meaning: Size spread shrinks toward a self-preserving shape.
insights.why_it_matters: Supports physics-based extrapolation of smoke properties.

insights.title: Still air changes the smoke
insights.evidence: Without flow (possible only in microgravity, where there is no buoyant plume) smoke had ×1.4–3.3 larger Dm and 7–18× fewer particles, and further aging changed it little because it had already coagulated near the heater.
insights.meaning: Without buoyancy, quiescent smoke is concentrated, coagulates fast and is coarse but dilute.
insights.why_it_matters: Smoke trapped in avionics boxes or stagnant corners will not look like ventilated smoke.

insights.title: Scattering and ionization detectors fail in opposite cases
insights.evidence: The two detection principles fail in opposite regimes. With 8 cm/s flow the ISS photoelectric (scattering) detector responded to 71% of pushes and the ionization chamber to 93%; for Kapton the ISS detector responded to only 27%. Without flow the ISS detector responded to 90% and the ionization chamber to 10%. Either detector would have responded to 95% of all pushes.
insights.meaning: Light scattering misses tiny particles; ionization misses dilute coarse smoke.
insights.why_it_matters: A single-principle detector leaves a blind spot.

insights.title: The Shuttle ionization detector also missed some smoke
insights.evidence: The Space Shuttle ionization smoke detector (powered in 9 pushes) alarmed in 6; it stayed silent for aged Kapton (test 70), a weak Teflon test (89) and a dilute lampwick test (92).
insights.meaning: Its alarm stayed silent for aged Kapton and weak tests.
insights.why_it_matters: Real flight hardware confirms the proxy-based pattern.

insights.title: A small model predicts size and detector response
insights.evidence: The AutoResearch-selected model predicts held-out Dm within a typical factor of 1.23 and M0 within 1.35, and reduces the detection Brier score by 51% relative to the prevalence; its combined score is 0.529 versus 1.043 for the mean baseline.
insights.meaning: Conditions predict Dm within ~23% and detection with half the error of a constant guess.
insights.why_it_matters: Gives a quick what-if tool for material, flow and transport time, within the tested range.

insights.title: TEM grids under-count small particles
insights.evidence: TEM image sizing of lampwick grids gives mean diameters ×1.7–2.7 the in-flight moment value: small particles and liquid droplets are under-counted on grids, so in-flight moments are the better number statistic.
insights.meaning: Image sizing gives larger means than in-flight moments.
insights.why_it_matters: In-flight moment instruments are preferable for number statistics.

insights.title: Measure at least two moments
insights.evidence: A single-moment detector is not enough for spacecraft: overheated wire insulation (Kapton, Teflon) in ventilated areas makes ~0.1 µm smoke that light scattering misses, while smoke trapped in still air (avionics boxes, stagnant corners) is dilute and coarse and weakens the ionization signal. Measuring two moments (e.g. the MPASS demonstrated on SAME-R, or combining ionization and scattering) covers both cases.
insights.meaning: Combining two size moments covers both blind spots.
insights.why_it_matters: Design recommendation for future spacecraft smoke detectors.

predictive_model.what_was_fitted: Ridge regression on material, a Brownian-coagulation variable ln(1+K·N0·t), no-flow and heater temperature for Dm, σg and M0 (Dg and AMD follow from Hatch–Choate); hierarchical beta-binomial detection rates by flow regime, material and aging.
predictive_model.formula_optional: y_j = ridge(material one-hot + ln(1 + K N0 t) + no_flow + 5(Rt/R0-1.35)), K N0 = 3.75e-3/s (x0.1 no-flow); Dg, AMD via Hatch-Choate; detection: P_j = beta-binomial rate in (flow, material, aged) -> (flow, material) -> flow regime -> global, a=2
predictive_model.evaluation: Leave-one-run-out (size) and leave-one-test-out (detection) cross-validation; 15 attempts by an AutoResearch loop editing only train.py.

score.meaning: Average of size NRMSE and detection Brier ratio; 1 ≈ predicting the average.

errors.meaning: A typical factor of 1.23 means predictions are usually within about ±23% of the measured value.

limitations: Valid only within the tested materials, aging times (36–1913 s) and flow regimes (0 or ~8 cm/s).
Detection targets are proxy thresholds, not flight alarm logic.
Best of 15 attempts on the same folds: mildly optimistic.
No validation on SAME-1 (PSI-102) or other flights.

habitat_relevance.iss_and_gateway: Directly relevant: microgravity, cabin-like air, and the ISS detector principle tested.
habitat_relevance.lunar_mars: Partial gravity restores some buoyancy, so quiescent-smoke effects should be weaker; not tested.
habitat_relevance.design_assumptions: Smoke amount was set by NASA for measurable signals; real fires vary.

unavailable_results.label: NASA-labelled material of 10 tests
unavailable_results.reason: No NASA table or TEM file names the material of tests 59, 61, 65, 66, 86, 90, 91, 99, 102, 103. They are heated tests; the heater fingerprint suggests silicone (59, 65, 66, 86, 91, 99, 103) or Kapton (61, 90, 102), reported in test_results[].material_inferred and not used in models.
